I've always thought the series tried to mesh strategy with the RPG aspects of leveling and learning about characters. My Castle seems to bring a few things to the table, and I think you have to look at some of it separately.  It's adding greater depth to the character interactions, whether or not you care for it in general or the particular way it's providing it, that portion of it is putting more focus on the "character study" aspect of the series while adding onto the "base" aspect. And I'm talking more barracks convo's, supports, being able to talk to your units. Not so much the social link feature.  It's adding a player housing concept, which should benefit the feeling of lordliness for a specific game. One thing it seems to be focusing on is resource management, which was one of the main criticisms of dropping weapon durability. Depending on how we get these resources, it could be a big deal or it could be a side thing. It's really hard to say how this will turn out, particularly because we don't know much about how we get the resources in the first place. And we can't tell how important that aspect is to the main game. Finally, and I think this is a big one. It's going to provide a ton of non-maingame content. And probably a good amount of end game content as well. I'm really looking forward to the idea of defending the base I've made, or fighting some of these spot pass teams. I don't think it's something that isn't with the spirit of the series, which I believe to be a strategy game wrapped in a pretty RPG bow. For me, the question is how much it's going to affect the actual strategy aspect of it, and how well it's going to do so. If done right this could simply provide a great amount of content and choices without diminishing the main game. > we lost the weapon triangle... They actually made it more dynamic. I'm actually very curious to see these new weapon changes in action. A lot of it seems to be an improved version of the old weight system, but adding some more unique effects. We'll have to wait and see how all these changes will play out, but they've made dramatic changes to the weapon system. It says to me that they weren't satisfied with the past few games and their systems, and they are making it more dynamic because of this. This is **not** something that will make it more accessible.  > If I can survive my first few games in the series, and I am bad at games in general, then I think it's not too difficult for most people to do so too. Now, first off, I just want to add those games having difficulty settings was them actually making the series more accessible, if I'm not mistaken, the first game to let you choose difficulty from the beginning was a specific entry. A specific entry seems to be the first that was made with this in mind, having three settings.  My main takeaway from what you said was the word survive, which is how I would describe my early playthroughs. My point is that not everyone will pick up a game as fast, and not everyone is willing to work past the frustration. Adding easier difficulties can benefit new comers without taking much away and things like Casual/Phoenix mode are them saving the time of adding another difficulty. Instead of making an even easier mode, they can just add Casual mode and call it a day. If you ask me, Casual mode was a great addition, and I don't think I've ever used it.  Edit: Wow this got long. **TLDR**: I think My Castle can add some kewl stuff, I think they've made efforts to add more dynamics to the game and I think the series has a serious learning curve and things like Casual Mode help new players come in without being intimidated.

Roads increase movement range* but lowers avoid. If an enemy reaches the entrance to your main castle you lose the chapter. Male x Female units can marry, they gain 5 points while standing next to each other for each turn up to turn 50 of each chapter. At 500 points, they marry, but each pairing starts with a certain amount of points.  Check your units for the "talk" option for good items and dialogue. If you are getting uppercut'd a lot when you are trying to attack it's probably because you are going straight for his high strings(almost all of his are) too often and the opponent is keyed in on that.  You can combat this by getting a f1 jail out of the hit stun of d1, d2 or d3. You can armor, go for b3, use b1, use a random normal like f4, try to get more successful jumpins or go for a special. You just need to do something to get them to block and or get some respect up close. You have to stop them from low profiling you by making them respect your options. This can be difficult at times, the d1 into f1 is the most effective way IMO. For zoning, it depends on who you are playing, but Aftershock can typically help Tremor against zoning. Metallic and Crystal have their merits here but not as much as Aftershock, even less so for Crystal. Just don't keep throwing things out against every char. There's some chars you can be reckless against but most of the time you want to make calculated decisions with projectiles. Your two best projectiles across all variations are the boulder and the up rock. Ground pound and rock throw have their place too but those two are the big ones. Boulder is pretty fast and knocks people down where you can use EX ground pound. Aftershock can use air pound to apply more long distance pressure or counter zone. Challenge with up rock often(not when horribly unsafe), remember you can hold back* to aim at a person jumping in or running in.  The zoning in particular is something you just will get the hang of the more you play, really just need to get a feel for it.  Edit: For clarity

Using the close up rock(db3b) will hit people trying to run under it or jump in. If it's a hit in the air you get a free chance to EX ground pound. I mostly use a combination of Crystal and Aftershock but at this point I choose variation solely because of the matchup. I've started to play Metallic quite a bit in recent weeks. Aftershock is probably the best one to start with, he gains two new moves and everything else is the same as variationless Tremor. His delayed ground pound(dd1) is almost useless but his air dd1 is one of the best moves in the game. It lets Tremor counter zone with the best of them. But if I thought I could handle certain characters zoning I would play Crystal and Metallic every match.  All variations are really good, Tremor may have a couple big weaknesses but he makes up for it in so many ways. I made a long winded post about variations a few weeks ago, check it out if you want more info about it.
